overview: The file documents the negotiation, formalization, and later follow-up of a temporary United States–Japan arrangement for reciprocal recognition of merchant-vessel load-line certificates pending the entry into force of the 1930 International Load Line Convention. Beginning with Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes’s March 1931 report, the papers show how Japan’s unilateral recognition since 1922 of certificates issued by the American Bureau of Shipping was converted through an exchange of diplomatic notes into a reciprocal executive agreement. The correspondence also extended Japanese recognition to certificates issued under U.S. authority by the American Committee of Lloyd’s Register of Shipping and American representatives of Bureau Veritas. The bundle includes State Department correspondence, the published Executive Agreement Series text, a later embassy despatch completing the record, and a 1935 cross-reference concerning Japanese ratification and timber load lines.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 180 from Forbes on reciprocal load-line recognition
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Japan’s willingness to continue its 1922 recognition of American load-line certificates if the United States reciprocally recognizes Japanese certificates and marks.
subfiles.summary: Forbes recounts the embassy’s approach to the Japanese Government concerning a temporary arrangement pending the effectiveness of the 1930 International Load Line Convention. Shidehara explained that the 1922 practice had been a unilateral Japanese undertaking because the United States then lacked a load-line law, and he requested explicit American reciprocity. Forbes reports that he has assured Shidehara that Japanese load-line marks will be recognized and asks the Department to confirm that Japanese certificates will also be accepted; he also transmits Japanese load-line legislation and the exchanged notes.

subfiles.title: State Department consultation with Commerce on the proposed agreement
subfiles.from: William R. Castle Jr., for the U.S. Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Requests the Commerce Department’s views before authorizing recognition of Japanese load-line certificates.
subfiles.summary: The State Department forwards Forbes’s despatch and its enclosures to the Secretary of Commerce. It concludes that the two governments appear to be in substantial agreement and proposes telegraphing approval of the ambassador’s assurances. An early Commerce Department response is requested before the instruction is sent to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 142 to Forbes on completing the agreement
subfiles.from: Harvey H. Bundy, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.to: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Directs Forbes to confirm American recognition of Japanese certificates and obtain recognition for additional American classification societies.
subfiles.summary: The Department authorizes Forbes to confirm that the United States will recognize Japanese load-line certificates and marks and that it accepts Japan’s continued recognition of American Bureau of Shipping certificates. It also directs him to notify Japan that Lloyd’s Register’s American Committee and American representatives of Bureau Veritas are authorized in particular cases to mark American vessels and issue certificates. Forbes is asked to forward any additional notes exchanged with the Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: Executive Agreement Series No. 25 front matter
subfiles.about: Identifies the published exchange of notes constituting the United States–Japan load-line agreement and supplies filing information.
subfiles.summary: The cover presents the arrangement as Executive Agreement Series No. 25, effected by notes dated February 13, March 19, March 30, August 25, and September 7, 1931. Publication No. 257 instructs users filing the Executive Agreement Series with the Treaty Series to place it after Treaty Series No. 840.

subfiles.title: Dooman note No. 46 proposing continuation of the 1922 arrangement
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.to: Kijūrō Shidehara, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Asks Japan to continue the 1922 load-line arrangement pending implementation of the international convention.
subfiles.summary: Dooman informs Shidehara that the United States has enacted a load-line law effective September 2, 1930. He asks whether Japan will continue the 1922 arrangement until the 1930 convention enters into force. He encloses American load-line regulations and requests Japanese laws and regulations, preferably with official English translations.

subfiles.title: Shidehara note No. 30/C1 requesting reciprocal recognition
subfiles.from: Kijūrō Shidehara, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Explains that the 1922 undertaking was unilateral and requests American recognition of Japanese certificates and marks.
subfiles.summary: Shidehara clarifies that Japan alone undertook obligations in 1922 because the United States had not yet enacted a ship load-line law. He proposes that Japan continue recognizing certificates issued by the American Bureau of Shipping while the United States recognizes certificates and marks approved by competent Japanese authorities or designated associations. Japan will provisionally continue the earlier practice while awaiting a reply, and Shidehara transmits Japanese load-line laws and ordinances with translations.

subfiles.title: Forbes note No. 59 recognizing Japanese load-line marks
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.to: Kijūrō Shidehara, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Assures Japan that the United States recognizes load-line marks approved by the Japanese Government.
subfiles.summary: Forbes replies to Shidehara’s March 19 note. He acknowledges Japan’s continued recognition of American Bureau of Shipping certificates and states that the United States is recognizing load-line marks approved by Japan.

subfiles.title: Forbes note No. 136 confirming and broadening the arrangement
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.to: Kijūrō Shidehara, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Formally confirms reciprocal recognition and requests Japanese acceptance of certificates from Lloyd’s Register and Bureau Veritas representatives.
subfiles.summary: Forbes reports that Washington has confirmed the assurances contained in his March 30 note and has accepted Japan’s proposal to continue recognizing American Bureau of Shipping load lines. He adds that the United States authorizes the American Committee of Lloyd’s Register of Shipping and American representatives of Bureau Veritas to mark vessels and issue certificates in particular cases. Japan is asked to recognize certificates from those bodies when issued under U.S. authority.

subfiles.title: Shidehara’s acceptance of additional American certificates
subfiles.from: Kijūrō Shidehara, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Accepts certificates issued under U.S. authority by Lloyd’s Register and Bureau Veritas and requests specimens.
subfiles.summary: Shidehara acknowledges Forbes’s notes of March 30 and August 25 and accepts certificates issued to American ships by the American Committee of Lloyd’s Register and American representatives of Bureau Veritas, provided they are issued under U.S. governmental authority. For reference, he requests specimens or copies of the certificates. This reply completes the exchange constituting the reciprocal arrangement.

subfiles.title: Embassy despatch transmitting the final exchanged notes
subfiles.from: Elvin L. Mair, U.S. Embassy in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards the August 25 and September 7 notes and declares the embassy’s correspondence on the agreement complete.
subfiles.summary: The embassy transmits its note No. 136 of August 25 and the Japanese Foreign Office’s reply No. 97/C1 of September 7. Mair states that these documents, together with those enclosed with Forbes’s March 30 despatch, constitute the complete embassy–Foreign Office correspondence concerning the reciprocal load-line agreement.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to 1935 Commerce Department letter
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to another file for a Commerce Department inquiry about Japanese ratification and timber load lines.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to file 585.61 B 1/425 for a Commerce Department letter dated February 8, 1935. That letter requested an inquiry into whether Japan had ratified the convention or had authorized the inclusion of timber load lines in its national regulations.

interest: The file provides an unusually complete documentary trail showing how a unilateral administrative accommodation dating from 1922 became a reciprocal executive agreement after the United States enacted its own load-line law. The successive drafts, instructions, diplomatic notes, and published agreement make it possible to distinguish recognition of government-approved marks from recognition of certificates and to trace the addition of private classification societies acting under state authority. The 1935 cross-reference is also useful because it shows that unresolved questions about ratification and specialized timber load lines persisted after the agreement was concluded.
